strengths: Introduces a well-motivated 'information asymmetry' technique for scalable, low-cost synthesis of long-horizon computer-use tasks (simple to generate via forward chaining of subtasks, hard to solve as composed), which is a genuinely useful contribution for benchmark/dataset creation.

Comprehensive and clearly engineered pipeline with six specialized LLM agents (proposer, executor, verifier, reviser, follow-up proposer, summarizer), with full prompts provided in the appendix for reproducibility.

Strong empirical demonstration of benchmark difficulty and discriminative power: success rates of SOTA agents drop sharply (18%→4%) with increasing difficulty level, while a human baseline achieves 70% on the hardest tier, clearly establishing headroom for future work.
Thorough cost analysis showing ~$0.60/trajectory, orders of magnitude cheaper than human-curated datasets (τ-bench, OSWorld, TheAgentCompany), with transparent calculation details in the appendix.
Human evaluation of task/trajectory quality (feasibility, subtask coherence, persona relevance, verifier accuracy) all exceed 80%, lending credibility to the automated pipeline.
Demonstrates generality by successfully porting the pipeline to a different environment (InSTA web agents), showing the approach is not tied to a single simulator.
Good qualitative failure-mode analysis (mis-clicks, poor state tracking, lack of error recovery) that is useful for the community.
Detailed dataset statistics (token counts, step counts, software/domain diversity) support claims of long-horizon, multi-application task diversity.
weaknesses: Potential circularity in evaluation: the same LLM-based verifier used to determine task success/failure during data generation is also used as the ground-truth judge for benchmarking agent performance, and its own accuracy is only ~89% (per a separate small human-validated sample), which could bias reported success rates, especially at near-zero success levels where a few verifier errors substantially change reported numbers.

Small evaluation sample sizes: only 50 tasks per difficulty level for the main benchmark and only 20 tasks for the human baseline; given success rates as low as 2-4%, these samples correspond to very few (1-2) successful trajectories, undermining statistical reliability of the headline difficulty-drop claims.

The paper conflates task 'difficulty' with task horizon/length (number of chained subtasks); the authors acknowledge this but do not empirically disentangle intrinsic complexity from mere step count or novelty/familiarity effects.

All task generation relies solely on GPT-4.1, so the diversity/realism/complexity of generated tasks may reflect idiosyncrasies or biases of a single model family; the paper explicitly flags this as unexplored rather than testing it.

Despite the title emphasizing 'generalist computer-use agents' and claims that the dataset is well-suited for training, no training or fine-tuning experiments are actually conducted; this central motivating claim remains unsubstantiated and relegated to future work.

Baseline agents are evaluated with minimal scaffolding ('bare' LLMs prompted for pyautogui code), which is explicitly framed as a lower bound but makes it unclear how much of the observed difficulty reflects the benchmark itself versus weak agent scaffolding, limiting interpretability of the absolute numbers.

No ablation comparing AgentSynth's chained-subtask strategy against simpler/naive synthetic generation baselines, making it hard to isolate the specific benefit of the information-asymmetry design versus just having any automated pipeline.

Table 4's qualitative comparison categories (e.g., 'multi-domain', 'scalable') are somewhat subjectively defined by the authors themselves, which slightly weakens the objectivity of the claimed advantages over prior benchmarks.
Long subtask chains could accumulate drift away from the original persona or introduce incoherence, which is not rigorously quantified beyond the single 100-sample human quality check.

strengths: The core idea of exploiting information asymmetry (subtasks are easy to generate/verify but hard when composed) is a clean, well-motivated mechanism for producing scalable, difficulty-controllable benchmarks without human annotation.

Extensive validation of the automatic verifier: human agreement study (Table 1), calibration curves against human-judged completion scores across difficulty levels (Fig. 2), and an adversarial stress test with near-miss vs. benign perturbations (Table 2), which meaningfully addresses known concerns about LLM-based judges (Lu et al., 2025).

Thorough ablations beyond the main benchmark: comparison against a direct-instruction baseline isolating the effect of information asymmetry (Table 5), sensitivity analysis to the choice of base generator model (Table 6), and evaluation with multiple agent scaffolds (bare LLM, Agent S2.5, Agent S3) across several backbones (o4-mini, GPT-4.1, GPT-5, GPT-5.1).
Strong cost/scalability argument with a transparent cost breakdown ($0.6/trajectory, $0.1/task) compared against realistic human-annotation cost estimates for τ-bench, OSWorld, and TheAgentCompany.
Generality demonstrated by porting the pipeline to a second, structurally different environment (InSTA web agent), showing the same qualitative difficulty-scaling trend.

Good reproducibility support: full prompt templates for all six agent roles, action-space statistics, and detailed dataset statistics (horizon, app count, switches, memory span) that substantiate the difficulty-scaling claims.

Clear empirical result showing steep performance degradation of SOTA multimodal LLM agents with increasing task difficulty, and a large human-vs-agent performance gap (70% vs <20%), demonstrating discriminative power of the benchmark.
weaknesses: The paper's stated motivation includes both training and evaluating agents, but no experiments show the generated data actually improves agent training/fine-tuning performance downstream; the contribution is essentially an automatically-generated benchmark rather than a demonstrated data-generation-for-training pipeline.

The same automatic verifier is used both to filter/accept subtasks during data generation and to score agent success during evaluation, creating a potential circularity that could bias reported success rates in ways not fully disentangled by the (still limited, ~100-sample) human validation study.

Task difficulty is controlled essentially through a single knob (number of chained subtasks/horizon); other complexity axes (e.g., fine-grained visual discrimination) are measured but not directly manipulated, and the paper does not analyze whether performance drops are driven by genuine reasoning/planning difficulty vs. compounding low-level GUI grounding errors (which the failure-mode analysis suggests may dominate).

Persona-conditioned generation and LLM summarization may introduce systematic artifacts or reduce genuine semantic diversity; diversity claims rely mainly on surface statistics (app/domain distribution, token counts) rather than deeper analysis of task novelty or redundancy across the 6,000+ generated tasks.

Statistical rigor in the main results is uneven — Figure 4 (primary benchmark result) lacks confidence intervals/error bars for the reported success rates (only later figures like S3 comparisons include them), making it harder to assess significance of small differences between difficulty levels or models.

The comparison between AgentSynth and the direct-instruction baseline (Table 5) is somewhat confounded, since AgentSynth's pipeline includes revision/partial-credit mechanisms not present in the one-shot baseline, making the generation-success-rate comparison less of an apples-to-apples test of information asymmetry alone.

Novelty is somewhat incremental relative to related synthetic-data works cited (e.g., Learn-by-interact, OS-Genesis, AgentTrek), with the main differentiator being the specific subtask-chaining-then-summarizing mechanism rather than a fundamentally new technique.

strengths: The core idea of exploiting information asymmetry (easy to generate/execute step-by-step vs. hard to solve as a composed long-horizon task) is a clean and well-motivated mechanism for controllable difficulty generation, and is empirically validated via the ablation comparing AgentSynth to a direct-instruction baseline (Table 5), which nicely shows the intended decoupling between generation success and evaluation success.

The paper includes an unusually thorough battery of validation experiments for a synthetic-data paper: human quality evaluation (Table 1), verifier calibration against human judgments across difficulty levels (Fig. 2), and an adversarial stress test of the verifier with near-miss/benign perturbations (Table 2), which meaningfully strengthens confidence in the automatic evaluation pipeline.

Strong empirical results demonstrating a steep, monotonic difficulty gradient across six levels for multiple frontier models (o4-mini, GPT-4.1, Gemini-2.5-Pro, Claude-3.7), plus scaffolding experiments (Agent S2.5/S3) and a base-generator robustness study (Table 6), giving a fairly complete picture of how difficulty, model choice, and scaffolding interact.

Cost analysis is detailed and favorably compares against several human-annotated benchmarks (tau-bench, OSWorld, TheAgentCompany), and the pipeline is also demonstrated on a second, different environment (InSTA web agent) to show generality beyond OSWorld.
Full prompt templates and pipeline details are provided in the appendix, supporting reproducibility, along with a promise to release code/data.
weaknesses: The evaluation success rates reported throughout the paper (Fig. 4, 5, Tables 5, 6) rely entirely on the paper's own LLM-based verifier rather than human judgment at scale; although calibration is checked on a modest sample (100 instances, ~16 per difficulty level), this is a fairly small sample to certify verifier reliability at the higher, sparser difficulty levels where success is already near-zero, raising concern about noise/bias in the headline numbers.

There is a degree of circularity in the pipeline: the same or closely related model families (GPT-4.1/GPT-5 family) are used for task proposal, execution, verification, and (in some experiments) evaluation, which could introduce systematic biases favoring or disadvantaging certain task styles that are not independently checked against a truly external verification signal.

The long-horizon 'composed' tasks are essentially summarized concatenations of independently generated subtasks; it is unclear how much genuine interdependency/compositional reasoning this requires versus simply executing a sequence of loosely related actions in order, which affects how meaningfully the benchmark measures 'long-horizon planning' rather than 'many independent short tasks in a row.'

The comparison to prior benchmarks in Table 4 is largely qualitative (checkmarks for multi-domain/scalable/long-horizon) without deeper quantitative benchmarking against task complexity metrics used by those prior works, making the claimed superiority somewhat asserted rather than rigorously demonstrated.

The novelty relative to closely related prior work that also composes atomic/simple tasks into harder ones (e.g., Boisvert et al. 2024 WorkArena++, OS-Genesis, Learn-by-interact) is only partially differentiated in the related work section; the core 'generate easy, compose hard' idea is incremental rather than fundamentally new.

Task execution is capped at 10 steps per subtask and the bare-LLM evaluation setup is intentionally minimal (no fine-tuning, no scaffolding for baseline results), which conflates 'benchmark difficulty' with 'weak baseline agent design,' making it harder to disentangle whether steep performance drops reflect genuine task hardness or artifacts of a deliberately handicapped evaluation protocol.

Some auxiliary metrics introduced in the appendix (e.g., 'memory span', 'fine-grained percentage' in Table C.1) lack a clear, reproducible definition of how they are computed, limiting the interpretability of the complexity-scaling claims.
The claimed scalability to 'tens of thousands of tasks' is asserted but not empirically demonstrated at that scale within the paper; only ~6,000 tasks were actually generated and analyzed.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated core idea: exploiting information asymmetry between forward generation (easy) and evaluation (hard) to synthesize long-horizon computer-use tasks that are cheap to generate but genuinely difficult to solve.

Extensive and thoughtful supporting analyses beyond the main benchmark: verifier calibration against human judgment, an adversarial stress test of the verifier (near-miss vs. benign perturbations), and human inter-rater agreement (Cohen's kappa) on quality metrics.

Strong ablation studies that isolate the contribution of the proposed method: a direct-instruction baseline showing the asymmetry effect (flat generation success vs. steep evaluation drop for AgentSynth, vs. the opposite pattern for one-shot long-horizon generation), and robustness checks across different base generator models (GPT-4.1, GPT-5-mini, GPT-5, GPT-5.1).
Demonstrates generality of the pipeline by applying it to a second, structurally different environment (InSTA web agent), showing consistent difficulty scaling trends.

Good evaluation breadth across multiple SOTA backbones (o4-mini, GPT-4.1, Gemini-2.5-pro, Claude-3.7, GPT-5/5.1) and multiple agent scaffolds (bare LLM, Agent S2.5, Agent S3), showing the difficulty trend is robust to scaffolding choices.
Cost-efficiency and scalability are clearly quantified and compared against several human-annotated datasets, supporting the claimed practical value of the pipeline.
Reasonably strong reproducibility support: full prompt templates, action space, and cost-accounting details are included in the appendix.
weaknesses: The paper's title and framing emphasize task generation 'for generalist computer-use agents' and motivate the work partly around training data for agents, but no experiments actually show that training/fine-tuning an agent on AgentSynth trajectories improves downstream performance — the empirical contribution is essentially a benchmark plus a data-generation method, not a demonstrated training benefit.

The automatic LLM-based verifier used for pipeline construction is also used to score all model evaluations in Section 5, creating a degree of circularity; despite the calibration and adversarial stress-test analyses, an 88% agreement rate with humans (and 12% false-negative-avoidance rate under near-miss perturbations) could still meaningfully shift the already very low success-rate numbers (4-18%) reported for SOTA models.

Evaluation sample sizes are fairly small (50 tasks per difficulty level for the main benchmark, 20 tasks for the human baseline), and no confidence intervals/error bars are reported for the primary Figure 4 results, limiting the statistical strength of claims about steep performance drop-off.

Task difficulty is controlled almost exclusively via number of chained subtasks (horizon); while the paper shows other properties (apps, memory span, switches) scale together, this conflation makes it hard to disentangle whether harder levels are more challenging due to genuine reasoning complexity or simply longer execution/compounding-error exposure.

Task generation relies solely on OpenAI models (GPT-4.1 family) for the main dataset and prompts are fairly constrained (avoiding logins, emails, forms), which may bias the diversity and realism of the resulting persona-driven tasks toward a narrow style, despite the qualitative examples looking reasonable.

The comparison table (Table 4) qualitatively marks AgentSynth favorably on nearly all axes (multi-domain, scalable, long-horizon) in a somewhat self-serving binary fashion without a more nuanced discussion of any remaining limitations relative to prior benchmarks.
